big_idea: 1¢, 5¢, 10¢, 25¢. The same price can be paid in many coin combinations.
learning_intention: We are learning to name the four Canadian coins to 25¢ and to pay for a snack using the right coins.
student_learning_goal: I can name the four Canadian coins and pick coins to pay for snacks priced 5¢, 10¢, or 25¢.
success_criteria: I can name penny, nickel, dime, and quarter.
I can tell the value of each coin.
I can pay for a 5¢, 10¢, or 25¢ snack with the right coins.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Our Coin Counters Words' with 4 rows: PENNY 1¢, NICKEL 5¢, DIME 10¢, QUARTER 25¢. Add the embossed image (maple leaves, beaver, Bluenose, caribou) beside each row.
Real or printed Canadian coins (per pair: 10 pennies, 6 nickels, 5 dimes, 4 quarters)
Quincy piggy-bank cardstock cut-out, propped beside the Snack Shop
Snack Shop sign showing 3 prices: pizza slice 25¢, popcorn 10¢, lollipop 5¢
Lesson 5 formative tracker (Coin Recognition + Payment) — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Quincy the piggy-bank has a special belly full of coins — and not all of them are the same.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Quincy and the estimation jar with mixed coins inside.

'Friends — Quincy has been collecting coins all year. Today we're going to look inside and see what's there.' Tip the jar onto a tray slowly. 'Look! Some coins are big, some are small. Some are copper, some are silver. Are they all the SAME?' (No.) 'Right. There are FOUR kinds of Canadian coins we use to 25 cents. Let me introduce them.'

Pick up a penny. 'This is a PENNY. It is copper-coloured and it is worth ONE cent. We write 1¢.' Hold it up so every child sees. Add it to the chart's PENNY row.

Pick up a nickel. 'This is a NICKEL. It is silver and it is THICK. It is worth FIVE cents — 5¢. Look on the back — there is a BEAVER.' Add to the chart.

Pick up a dime. 'This is a DIME.
student_actions: Listen and watch as each coin is introduced.
Repeat each coin name aloud as a class.
Read the value off the chart after each addition.

action.activity_name: Coin Sort, Coin Match, and the Snack Shop

steps.instruction: Coin Sort station. Each pair gets a mixed pile of all four coin types and four labelled trays (PENNY, NICKEL, DIME, QUARTER). Sort by coin type. Then count each tray and record the count.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Sort your coin pile into the four trays. Then count each tray. How many pennies do you have? How many nickels?' Walk around. Watch for the dime/nickel confusion (silver-vs-silver). Use the size cue: dime is SMALLER than nickel.

steps.instruction: Coin Value Match station. A 4-row mat shows '1¢ ___ 5¢ ___ 10¢ ___ 25¢ ___'. Children place the matching coin on each row.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'On this mat, you'll see four prices: 1, 5, 10, 25. Pick the right coin for each. Read it back to your partner.' Watch for the bigger-means-more error: a child placing a quarter on the 5¢ row because it's the biggest. Redirect to the chart.

steps.instruction: Pay-the-Price station with Snack Shop cards (M5). The pair has the 3 price-tag cards (pizza 25¢, popcorn 10¢, lollipop 5¢) and a tray of mixed coins. Take turns: one is the cashier, one is the customer. Customer picks the right coin to pay for each snack.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You're going to take turns being the cashier and the customer. Customer picks the snack, then puts down the right coin to pay. Cashier checks. Switch.' Walk around. Watch for: did the customer use ONE coin (e.g. a dime for popcorn) or BUILD the price from multiple coins (e.g. two nickels = 10¢ for popcorn)?

steps.instruction: Stretch round (only if Step 3 went smoothly): the customer must pay for the snack ANOTHER way. Popcorn = 10¢ = one dime OR two nickels OR ten pennies OR a nickel and five pennies. The cashier checks each combination.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Popcorn costs 10 cents. You used one DIME. Now pay another way!' Watch for which children naturally see two-nickels-equals-a-dime (the strongest A6.13/A6.11 connection).

steps.instruction: Whole-class debrief and summative worksheet. Bring children back to the carpet. Distribute the summative Coin Counters worksheet (3 priced items, multiple-choice grid). They complete it independently while the teacher records the formative tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You've all run the Snack Shop! Last thing: a small worksheet that shows what you learned. Three snacks, three prices. Circle the right coin for each.' Walk around. Tick each child's row on the tracker for: coin recognition (Step 1), value match (Step 2), single-coin payment (Step 3), multi-coin combination (Step 4), worksheet score.

differentiation.for_emerging: These children stay at the Coin Sort station for both rotations and skip the Pay-the-Price station. The sort is concrete enough that they can master coin recognition without the added load of value matching.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch coin-combination cards: 'Pay 25¢ using ONLY nickels and dimes (no quarter).' Forces composition (2 dimes + 1 nickel = 25¢). Stays inside A6.13 with stretch into A6.11/A6.12.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a coin-name picture card the child can point to. Also provide a tactile sort: real coins (not printed) so the size and weight differences are physical. The dime-vs-nickel confusion is helped enormously by handling real coins.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Coin Hunt floor version: the four coin trays are placed at four corners of the room. The teacher calls a value ('TEN cents!') and children run to the matching corner. Repeat for all four values.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child name each coin by sight (no chart prompt)? Can they say the value of each coin? Can they pay for a snack with a single matching coin? Can they pay another way using a coin combination (stretch)?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker for each child as they rotate through stations. The summative worksheet score (out of 3) goes in the last column.
tracker_columns: Names penny / nickel / dime / quarter on sight
Pays for snack with single matching coin
Pays for snack with multi-coin combination (stretch)

discussion_prompts: Which coin was your favourite to learn? Why?
Which coin tricked you the most? Why?
If you had to pay for a 25¢ pizza but you didn't have a quarter, what could you use?
Outside school, when do you see coins?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child holds up the coin matching what the teacher names: 'Show me a NICKEL.' (Children hold up a nickel.) 'Show me a DIME.' Round through all four. Then a final closing chant: 'Penny ONE, Nickel FIVE, Dime TEN, Quarter TWENTY-FIVE!' Each child returns their coin set to the tray and lines up at the door.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Coin Recognition + Payment tracker for A6.13 (per-station), plus the completed summative Coin Counters worksheet (multi-choice).
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's CAPSTONE. A6.13 is the headline expectation; the tracker covers all four substages (recognise / state value / pay with single coin / pay with combination). The worksheet captures A6.13 explicitly and A6.11/A6.12 implicitly (one prompt asks for a 5¢ + 5¢ = 10¢ combination — testing additive composition of coin values).

expanded_walkthrough.title: Bigger means more — repairing the dime/nickel size-vs-value confusion
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common K trap on A6.13 is the size-vs-value confusion: the dime is the SMALLEST coin but worth MORE than the bigger nickel. Children's everyday rule 'bigger means more' is reinforced everywhere (bigger cookie = more cookie, bigger cube tower = more cubes, taller person = older), so the dime is genuinely counter-intuitive. Step 1 (Coin Sort) is where this confusion shows up — a child looks at a nickel and a dime, sees that the nickel is BIGGER, and concludes the nickel is worth more. Without intervention, every payment task downstream will fail. The script below covers the side-by-side compare that breaks the size rule, and why the embossed image is the long-term anchor.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: The pair has just finished sorting their coins. Their PENNY tray has 6 pennies, NICKEL tray has 3 nickels, DIME tray has 2 dimes, QUARTER tray has 1 quarter. The teacher walks up. The child (call her Maya) is asked which tray is worth the most TOTAL value. She picks the QUARTER tray (correct — 25¢) but for the WRONG REASON: she points at the size of the quarter coin. Then the teacher asks her to compare a single nickel and a single dime side by side.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside Maya. Place one nickel and one dime on the table side by side. 'Look at these two coins. Which is bigger?' She points at the nickel. 'Right — the nickel is bigger. Now which is worth more?' Watch her face. She'll usually say 'the nickel' confidently, because bigger means more.

Don't correct yet. Pick up the dime. 'Read what it says on the dime.' She reads '10 cents'. Pick up the nickel. 'Read what it says on the nickel.' She reads '5 cents'. Now ask again: 'Which is worth more — 5 or 10?' She'll usually say 10. 'And which COIN was 10?' (The dime — the smaller one.) 'YES. Which is worth more — the bigger coin or the smaller coin?' (The smaller. Pause.) 'That feels wrong, doesn't it?'

This is the magical moment. 'Coin size DOESN'T tell us value. The NUMBER on the coin does. The dime is smaller but the number on it is BIGGER. The number wins.' Hold up the chart. 'Look — when we read the chart, we read the NUMBERS, not the size. Penny ONE, Nickel FIVE, Dime TEN, Quarter TWENTY-FIVE.'

The long-term anchor: every coin has a unique embossed image (penny → maple leaves, nickel → beaver, dime → Bluenose, quarter → caribou). 'When you can't remember the value, look at the picture on the BACK. Beaver = 5. Bluenose ship = 10. Caribou = 25.' This pictorial anchor is more durable than the colour or size cue, because the colour/size of nickel and dime are too similar.

Watch Maya in Step 3 (Pay-the-Price). If she tries to pay 10¢ for popcorn with a nickel, she's still confused — redirect to the chart. If she correctly picks a dime, tick 'states value' on the tracker.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) 'The nickel is bigger so it's worth more.' Hasn't separated size from value. Most common K starting point.
(Mid) After the side-by-side reveal, says 'oh — the dime is worth more because of the number'. But may still slip on the next round when not watching the numbers.
(Strong) Without prompting, says 'the dime is worth more even though it's smaller because the number is bigger'. Has internalised value-by-number.
(Stretched) Volunteers: 'And the QUARTER is worth more than the dime even though they're both silver — the quarter has 25.' Has generalised the rule across all silver coins.
common_misconceptions: Bigger coin means more value. (The dime is the canonical counter-example. Repair: side-by-side compare with the value numbers prominent.)

Silver coins are all worth the same. (Some children lump nickel + dime + quarter into a 'silver' category and conclude they all have one value. Repair: hold all three side by side and read the embossed value off each.)

The penny is special because it's a different colour. (True — but children sometimes assume the colour DETERMINES value, so they doubt the rule when they see a copper-coloured 1¢ next to silver coins. Repair: emphasise that colour is a CLUE, not a rule.)
recovery_moves: Always anchor to the embossed image. Beaver = 5, Bluenose = 10, caribou = 25. The picture is more reliable than the colour or size — and is the long-term cue when the child encounters older or worn coins.
Use side-by-side comparisons EVERY time. Don't show coins one at a time; always lay them out together so the relative size and the relative value are both visible.
Practise payment to ONE price ('pay 10¢') with all the coin combinations the price allows (1 dime; 2 nickels; 10 pennies; 1 nickel + 5 pennies). Composition reinforces value across coins.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice and summative evidence of A6.13 — recognising the four Canadian coins to 25¢, naming their values, and selecting the right coins to pay for priced items.

parts_outline.task: Coin recognition grid: 4 rows, each showing a coin image, a coin name, and a value. The child draws lines to match coin → name → value.

Three Snack Shop scenes (popcorn 10¢, lollipop 5¢, pizza 25¢). For each scene the child circles the correct coin (or coin combination) from a 4-option grid. One option per scene shows a multi-coin combination (e.g. 5¢ + 5¢ for popcorn) — circling that captures A6.11 / A6.12.
Empty 'Pay another way!' grid. The child draws three different coin combinations that all add to 10¢. Sentence starter: 'I can pay 10¢ as ___ + ___ = 10¢.'

expected_image_assets: Penny puppet thumbnail in the worksheet header
Canadian coin illustrations (penny, nickel, dime, quarter)
Snack Shop priced items (pizza, popcorn, lollipop)
Quincy the piggy-bank cheering icon in a corner
